list.listitem: For patients with reflux demonstrated by handheld Doppler, or if venous insufficiency is otherwise suspected, evaluation by duplex imaging is indicated to determine the extent and origins of venous reflux. C
Compression stockings may provide effective symptom relief for varicose veins but will not eliminate varicose veins. B
Treatment of primary varicose veins, including telangiectases and reticular veins by compression sclerotherapy appears to be effective. B
The efficacy of foam sclerotherapy relative to conventional sclerotherapy and surgery remains uncertain. B
Surgery or endovenous ablation are effective measures for limiting venous reflux, and eliminating varicose veins. B

background.definition: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous subcutaneous veins. They occupy the superficial venous system of the lower extremities. Varicose veins exceed 4 mm in diameter. Telangiectases and venulectases are dilatations of 2 mm or less. Nonpalpable varicosites of less than 4 mm are termed reticular veins; these are often found at the lateral thigh.

list.listitem: The overall incidence of varicose veins is about 14 per 1000 person years (8.5 for men and 19.2 for women).
In the United States, about 28% of women and 15% of men have varicose veins.
Primary disease: superficial venous insufficiency.

Secondary disease: venous hypertension may be transmitted from deep or perforating vein incompetence due to venous obstruction or from increased intraabdominal or pelvic pressure, for example, from tumor, or pregnancy. Extensive chronic varicosities may be seen with additional comorbid conditions like hepatic cirrhosis.
Venous insufficiency results from valve incompetence and reflux. Vein wall distention may be responsible for valve dysfunction.
Structural abnormalities in the vein wall, such as reduced elasticity, may allow distention of the vein. These properties may be inherited, secondary to alterations in enzyme expression and activity.
Venous insufficiency results in retrograde venous flow from proximal to distal and from deep to superficial via incompetent saphenous and perforating veins.

list.listitem: While the diagnosis of varicose veins is based on their visible presence, determining their relationship to underlying reflux at the junctions of the superficial and deep venous systems is critical in a complete assessment. C
Clinical tests are inaccurate in assessing underlying venous reflux. C
Handheld Doppler examination adequately screens for valvular incompetence. C
Venous duplex imaging assists in treatment decisions by identifying locations of venous reflux. C
Disease severity scoring for chronic venous insufficiency grades varicose veins based on size and distribution, while a segmental disease score is based on imaging.
Varicose veins may be asymptomatic or associated with aching pain, pressure, fatigue, and itching. Symptoms may diminish with elevation of the extremities, walking, and use of compression hose.

Inspection reveals dilated, tortuous veins along the course of the greater saphenous vein, long saphenous vein, or at the site of perforating veins. Varicosities become more visible and symptoms typically worsen with standing and in warmer temperatures.
Cutaneous signs and complications of venous stasis include erythema, hyperpigmentation, scaling, and ulceration.

Clinical tests, such as the cough, tap, Trendelenberg and Perthes tests, are inaccurate in assessing venous reflux. The tap test is best at ruling in and a negative.The Perthes test is the best at ruling out, but neither is very useful.
Handheld Doppler testing is an adequate screening test for valvular incompetence.
Doppler ultrasound and tourniquet test accurately detects saphenofemoral incompetence.
Duplex imaging identifies venous insufficiency or thrombosis. Duplex mapping may guide management, especially involving recurrent varicosities.
In general, diagnosis and treatment are guided by the presence and magnitude of symptoms and by the extent to which they are a manifestation of chronic venous insufficiency.
Supplementing the history and physical examination with additional diagnostic tests decreases the rate of surgical referrals.
Clinical assessment is poorly sensitive compared to venous duplex examination in detecting deep venous reflux.
Symptoms of varicose veins are reduced with the use of compression stockings. B
Injection sclerotherapy improves symptoms associated with varicose veins and appears to improve venous hemodynamics, but there is low evidence that this treatment is better than placebo. B

Choice of sclerosants and their formulation, the type and length of compression, do not significantly effect outcome. A This finding was confirmed with a recent review of 17 randomized controlled trials.

Surgery provides symptom relief and improves quality of life for patients with uncomplicated varicose veins. There is insufficient evidence to preferentially recommend surgical therapy or sclerotherapy. B
Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) therapy have compared favorably to surgery. B

Surgery is indicated for treatment of larger varicosities (>4-6 mm), incompetent perforators, and reflux at the saphenofemoral and saphenopopliteal junctions. It improves symptoms and quality of life compared to conservative management. A systematic review found that outcomes were similar for open surgery, laser, and radiofrequency techniques, although return to work may be faster with the latter.

Traditional surgery consists of ligating the saphenous vein alone or in combination with removal of the vein by stripping. Ligation of the saphenofemoral junction and other sites of reflux with or without endovascular sclerotherapy is associated with a lower rate of recurrent reflux after 10 years compared to endovascular sclerotherapy alone.

A systematic review of 73 studies including 45 RCTs was performed to support guidelines from the American Vein and Lymphatic Society. The authors concluded that high ligation and stripping (HLS) had higher 30 day and 5 year closure rates than both radiofrequency ablation and ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (UGFS). No difference was seen between endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) and HLS. Thermal treatments had a lower risk of recurrence than UGFS but was also associated with worse quality of life scores.

Sclerotherapy is used primarily to treat reticular veins, and residual varicosities following surgical therapy. It is effective in relieving symptoms and improving venous hemodynamics. Surgery and sclerotherapy have comparable outcomes in the treatment of primary varicose veins.
Laser ablation may be superior to foam sclerotherapy or surgery as initial patients with symptomatic varicose veins >3 mm with saphenous vein reflux.

Injection sclerotherapy involves the injection of an irritant such as sodium tetradecyl sulfate, polidocanol, or hypertonic saline followed by venous compression. There are no differences in effectiveness of various agents. This is also true for agents used to treat telangiectasias.
Foam sclerotherapy, a mixture of a sclerosing agent and air, is administered under local anesthesia with ultrasound guidance. It is no more effective than other therapies.

A randomized clinical trial found that foam sclerotherapy was slightly less effective than laser or surgical therapy for varicose veins. A systematic review concluded that overall outcomes were similar amongst differing treatments.
A Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence that sclerotherarpy is effective and safe in treating varicose veins compared to placebo.

Endovenous RFA is a minimally invasive treatment done under local tumescent anesthesia with ultrasound guidance. While there are no differences in complications, patients treated with RFA return to activity within 1 day, return to work sooner, and report better quality of life than those treated with surgery. Outcomes in patients with venous ulcers (i.e., time to healing) may be improved by this intervention.

A trial randomized 280 patients to endothermal ablation or surgical ligation and stripping. At 10 years, 206 participants were still evaluable, with a lower recurrence rate in the endothermal ablation group (37% vs 59%, p = 0.005, NNT = 5).

EVLA uses lasers to heat the vein blood and wall, resulting in thrombotic occlusion. EVLA and and surgery have similar efficacy at 6 months as measured by quality of life scores, clinical severity scoring, and return to work and return to routine activity times. Postoperative pain and bruising were lower in the EVLA-treated patients.
A systematic review of 16 RCTs and 13 cohort studies concluded that endovenous radiofrequency ablation and laser ablation were comparable with regards to efficacy and complication rates.
RFA and EVLA are at least as effective as surgery in treating greater saphenous varicose veins.

A trial of 60 patients with bilateral varicose veins used EVLA in one leg and RFA in the other. Adverse effects such as edema (28% vs 66%), hyperemia (21% vs 31%) and ecchymosis (31% vs 52%) were less common with EVLA. Overall patient satisfaction was 52% with EVLA and 31% for RFA; 17% were equally satisfied with the two procedures.

A systematic review identified 28 studies with 2228 limbs comparing endovenous thermal ablation (EVTA), ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (UGFS), and surgery for treatment of recurrent varicose veins arising from the saphenous vein or saphenofemoral junction. Ultrasound detected recurrence rates were 4.3% (95% CI .4% to 10.8%) for EVTA, 11.2% (95% CI 6.8% to 16.4%) for UGFS, and 23.3% (95% CI 10.4 to 43.0%) for surgery. EVTA also had the lowest clinical recurrence rate (2.4%).
A systematic review found 10 RCTs with 1545 patients and concluded that compression has some benefit for pain but not for any other outcomes following thermal ablation of varicose veins.
Horse chestnut seed extract oral preparations appear to be effective in reducing signs and symptoms of chronic venous insufficiency.

Use of gradient compression stockings decreases symptoms of leg pain, swelling, and fatigue. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether compression stockings are adequate for the initial and sole treatment of varicose veins without ulceration.
A randomized trial with 206 patients undergoing endothermal ablation (with or without concurrent phlebectomy) found less short-term pain in those randomized to compression stockings post-operatively.
Compression by bandaging or stockings improves healing rates of venous leg ulcers.
Asymptomatic varicosities do not require therapy unless there are cosmetic concerns. C
Although family history confers risk for varicose veins, physical activity and weight control may prevent their emergence. C
Asymptomatic patients with uncomplicated varicosities should be reassured and encouraged to maintain appropriate weight and calf muscle tone. C

In registries, younger patients with varicose veins (ages 20-34) were noted to have a higher risk of deep vein thrombosis; there was no association noted with peripheral artery disease or pulmonary embolus.

A systematic review identified three studies. Rutosides, plant-derived flavinoids, reduces symptoms associated with varicose veins in pregnancy; however, safety has not been established. External compressions did not appear to be effective in one small study, while reflexology was.
There is no association between varicose veins during pregnancy and birth outcomes.
